title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Boston Scientific restarts shipping at its main distribution centres — nine days after an IT breach stopped production
items.content_text: Boston Scientific said on 3 September that it has begun restoring shipping for the majority of its products at its major distribution centres worldwide, nine days after a 25 August intrusion knocked out internal IT systems and stopped it manufacturing, processing orders and shipping devices. Working with CrowdStrike, the company says it now has growing confidence the unauthorised access was confined to select internal-facing on-premises infrastructure, that cloud systems were unaffected, and that it has seen no further unauthorised activity since 25 August. It has still not named an actor, confirmed ransomware, or set a date for full recovery. For plant managers the lesson is unchanged and uncomfortable: nothing published suggests a controller or DCS was reached, yet production stopped anyway, because the systems that tell a factory what to build and where to ship it sit on the IT side.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Boston Scientific press releases and SEC Form 8-K filing — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, MedTech Dive and HIPAA Journal
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident identified 25 Aug 2026; SEC Form 8-K 26 Aug 2026; latest company update 3 Sep 2026 restoring shipping at major distribution centres, no full-restoration date given

items.title: A phone call, not an exploit — McKesson’s SSO accounts were talked open, then used against Salesforce and Snowflake
items.content_text: McKesson disclosed on 31 August that it had discovered a cybersecurity incident on 25 August. The extortion group ShinyHunters claims responsibility, says it took roughly a terabyte over four days — about 284 million records — and demanded around $55 million; the company states it has not determined the incident to be material. The reported route in is the part worth studying: voice phishing against employees, leading to compromised Okta single sign-on accounts, and from there into the company’s Salesforce and Snowflake tenants. No software flaw was exploited. For a manufacturer the parallel is direct — MES, historian and quality data increasingly land in the same class of cloud analytics platform, reached with the same SSO, and the help desk that resets a plant engineer’s MFA is the same desk that was called here.
tags: Incident — Identity-based intrusion at a major distributor

items.title: A chip-programming supplier pulled its own production and shipping systems offline to contain ransomware
items.content_text: Data I/O, which builds the programming systems used to load firmware onto automotive and consumer electronics before assembly, detected ransomware on IT systems on 16 August and disclosed it in an 8-K filed with the SEC on 21 August. Containment involved taking systems offline, and the company said the outage affected shipping, manufacturing, production and support functions. More than 65% of its second-quarter business came from automotive electronics production. The point for a plant manager is second-order: this is a supplier whose downtime shows up as missing programmed parts on someone else’s line, and the disruption came from the containment decision as much as from the malware. The company has since said the incident was contained and systems restored.

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese scanning and relay platforms built out of other people’s IoT devices
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic appeared to come from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, but the relay design is the manufacturing lesson: unmanaged internet-connected devices in a plant — cameras, badge readers, HVAC controllers, machine-monitoring gateways — are exactly what these platforms recruited, and your firewall logs never showed who was really there.

items.title: Clop has named more than 40 PTC Windchill victims, and what it took is how your products are built
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations as victims of a campaign against internet-facing PTC Windchill product lifecycle management deployments, with manufacturing, aerospace and industrial suppliers among the confirmed names. Windchill is where design files, bills of material, supplier documentation, tolerances and change history live. Losing it is not a privacy incident. It is the disclosure of how a product is made, to whom it is sourced, and where the process is sensitive — and for firms whose competitive position rests on process knowledge rather than a patent, that is the whole asset. The campaign also demonstrates the pattern: attackers now go after the engineering record rather than the shop floor.

items.title: An attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from one operator’s site into another’s plant
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that started at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, where a turbine was taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both organisations bought from the same carrier. A private APN is an addressing and billing arrangement, not a security boundary: if the devices on it can reach one another, another subscriber’s compromised router becomes your ingress. Manufacturers should read this as a warning about a common convenience — the cellular links used for remote machine monitoring, OEM diagnostics, outbuildings, tank farms and satellite sites are frequently on exactly this kind of shared arrangement.
tags: Incident — Lateral movement across a shared carrier network

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect the plant — and a planning horizon of three months
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. Manufacturing is where the dependency map usually surprises people: MES scheduling, licence servers, recipe management, quality systems and label printing all sit on the enterprise side, so “cut IT and keep making product” frequently fails within a shift. That is the argument for pre-building separation points and testing them. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months of isolated operation is deliberately uncomfortable and worth using as a tabletop scenario rather than a target.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

items.title: An AI model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in hours — and bricked a third
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For a plant the uncomfortable part is the long tail: an exploit proven against one controller in a family is now cheaper to move onto the other variants sitting on your lines, which is exactly the population that never got patched because the CVE “did not apply to our model”.
tags: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

items.title: Fire Ant hijacks the routers and authentication servers sitting between the plant and everything else
items.content_text: Sygnia’s 30 August research puts the China-nexus actor it calls Fire Ant inside network infrastructure rather than on top of it: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts across a large interconnected estate. Router implants suppressed selected syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and served interactive shells that produced no records; on TACACS the actor injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as logins were approved. Sygnia reports scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks but does not confirm compromise there. Most plants do not run IOS XR. Most plants do depend on a corporate network team, an integrator or an MSP for the routers and the authentication service between the enterprise and the cell — and on those same devices’ logs to prove what happened.

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. No victims, actors or techniques are named. For a plant the useful part is the instruction not to assume OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. In discrete and process manufacturing that usually means a specific short list: the machine an OEM ships with its own 4G router for remote support, the line acquired with a business unit and never brought under the standard build, the engineering workstation dual-homed for convenience, and the cell that still speaks Modbus or unauthenticated S7comm because the migration project was deferred. It lands the same week five US agencies described AI-written scripts reading S7 controllers across critical manufacturing.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: A ransomware affiliate ran an AI coding agent inside victim networks — and the exposed server shows exactly how
items.content_text: CloudSEK published analysis on 27 August of a misconfigured server belonging to a Russian-speaking Aurora ransomware affiliate, exposing tooling, command history, credential material and the operator’s Cursor chat transcripts. The campaign ran from April to July 2026 across nine countries; the operator reached domain-level or interactive access at 17 organisations, and four appeared on Aurora’s leak site. Manufacturing, food, agriculture and professional-services organisations were among those affected. The notable detail is not that AI was used but where: the transcripts show the assistant helping plan Active Directory escalation and intrusion steps, compressing the time between initial access and domain control. For a manufacturer the practical question is whether the identity used by IT administrators can reach the engineering workstations and the MES, because this operator’s route was domain privilege, not an ICS exploit.
tags: Threat Intel — Ransomware tradecraft, AI-assisted intrusion

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intel — Ransomware tradecraft, AI-assisted intrusion

items.title: Manufacturing took 747 of the 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in the second quarter
items.content_text: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in Q2 2026, up around 12 percent on Q1, with manufacturing absorbing the clear majority. The analysis is blunt about mechanism: attackers did not need control-system access to stop production. Encrypting ERP, MES, quality systems, label printing, shipping and scheduling halts a line just as effectively as touching a PLC, and it is far easier. The Data I/O disclosure this month is the same story from the inside — production stopped as a containment decision on IT systems, not because a controller was manipulated. Manufacturers who scope OT security around the control network alone are defending the part attackers are not aiming at.
tags: Threat intel — Manufacturing share of industrial ransomware

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, with critical manufacturing named
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic resembling legitimate monitoring. Critical manufacturing is among the named sectors, and the agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than manipulation. The change worth internalising is not a new exploit. Writing a working S7 query used to require someone who knew the protocol; it no longer does, which enlarges the population capable of interrogating an exposed SIMATIC controller and makes obscurity a much weaker control than it was.
tags: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory naming critical manufacturing

items.title: CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is unusually direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Manufacturers recognise the pattern because engineering workstations, MES servers and corporate laptops so often share one Active Directory, and because plant-floor systems are frequently excluded from whatever monitoring exists on the grounds that alerts would be noisy.
tags: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch is aimed at the engineering workstation — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September, and the theme is the engineering workstation rather than the controller. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client: CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — and that machine is usually the same laptop holding project files, licences and cell credentials. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH pushes firmware to Logix controllers and communication modules, so it habitually runs as an account with broad reach into the cell. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects. None is reported as exploited.
tags: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
items.content_text: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition and the PaperCut security bulletin — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor disclosed active exploitation 27 Aug 2026; CVEs assigned 28 Aug 2026; added to KEV 31 Aug 2026

items.title: Rockwell fixes a weak password-hashing work factor in OTTO Fleet Manager — low drama, but it sits on the AMR control path
items.content_text: Rockwell has patched CVE-2026-75112 in OTTO Fleet Manager, the console that dispatches and monitors autonomous mobile robots on plant floors. The flaw is an insufficient work factor in the bcrypt implementation used to hash stored passwords — it does not hand anyone access on its own, but it makes offline brute-forcing of a stolen hash database materially cheaper. CISA scores it 6.8 (CVSSv3) / 6.9 (CVSSv4) and states it is not remotely exploitable, so this is a housekeeping item rather than an emergency. It earns a place on a manufacturing page for a different reason: fleet managers are a category of system that has quietly become operational. If someone recovers a fleet administrator credential, they are not reading reports — they are issuing movement commands to vehicles sharing floor space with people.
tags: Advisory — Autonomous mobile robot fleet management

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and after the Boston Scientific and Data I/O outages that is the pattern worth noticing: what stops manufacturing is usually the layer under it. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the MES server, historian, machine-vision appliance, protocol gateway and OT network sensor in most plants are Linux underneath, frequently as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s timetable. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory — directly relevant in manufacturing, where Artifactory commonly stages firmware, container images and automation packages that end up on the plant floor. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; exposed instances are usually unowned.
tags: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. On a plant network this is the database under the historian, the MES, the batch or recipe store and the quality system — frequently an instance a machine builder or integrator installed as part of a line and left at the build it shipped with, sitting on the same flat network as the engineering workstations. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, historian and MES databases

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance runs as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre saw indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept appeared. In manufacturing, NetScaler routinely fronts the remote access used by engineers, third-shift support and the machine builders who dial in to diagnose equipment.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access

items.title: Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
items.content_text: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. In a plant Veeam ONE usually watches the backups of the MES, the historian and the engineering workstations that hold your PLC project files — the recovery capability that decides whether a ransomware event costs you a shift or a fortnight. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs.
tags: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Veeam knowledge-base articles KB4905 and KB4892 — corroborated by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity News

items.title: The Git server holding your PLC projects just went into KEV — Gitea is being exploited in the wild
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, it lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July; exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea has become common in controls engineering because it is trivial to stand up inside a plant network for PLC projects, HMI screens, robot programs and configuration baselines. That convenience is the risk: a low-privilege contractor account converts into code execution on the machine holding the authoritative copy of your production logic. Federal remediation was due 28 August.

items.title: CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — unauthenticated code execution on a dual-homed device
items.content_text: Siemens’ August advisory set includes a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges. Ten Siemens advisories arrived in the batch alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact publications, and CISA published companion advisories the same week. The reason to prioritise this above other maximum-severity items is placement. Edge gateways are deployed specifically to move machine data from the line out to a historian, an analytics platform or an OEM cloud service, which makes them dual-homed by design and often the one device with a route in both directions.
tags: Advisory — Maximum severity, Siemens edge gateway

items.title: OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical-infrastructure operators — terms not yet published
items.content_text: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For manufacturers the interesting part is the timing rather than the money: the same week produced Forescout’s demonstration that a supervised model can re-target a working PLC exploit at a sibling controller in hours, which is the offensive mirror of what this programme proposes to subsidise. Note it, wait for eligibility terms, and if you later evaluate it, treat it as you would any third party seeking telemetry from an engineering or plant network — because that is the data such tooling needs to be useful.

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and your customers will hold you to it
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Manufacturers read this as a supplier, not as a victim: when an outage stops shipments, your customers’ production planning depends on how quickly and how honestly you can say what is affected and for how long. Boston Scientific’s late-August outage — which disrupted manufacturing, order processing and shipping — is the shape of the problem.

items.title: CISA publishes internet exposure reduction guidance — and the target list for this sector is engineering workstations, historian and MES bridges, OEM remote-support appliances on production machinery, and the cellular routers shipped inside packaged equipment
items.content_text: CISA released guidance on 26 August directing organisations to identify which of their systems are reachable from the internet, remove remote access that is not required, and harden whatever must stay externally accessible. It is deliberately unglamorous: an inventory step, a removal step and a hardening step, published in the same week the UK NCSC warned that internet-exposed OT and edge devices are being targeted with real-world disruption already caused. On a plant floor the exposure is rarely the PLC itself — it is the machine builder’s support appliance, the cellular router inside a packaged skid, or the historian bridge that was published so a corporate dashboard could reach it. Those arrive with the equipment and are commissioned by someone other than the security team. The guidance carries no deadline and applies to no one by force, which is precisely why it tends to be filed rather than executed.

items.title: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware — with a fuller report following. The obligation lands on the manufacturer, so it applies to industrial firms that build machinery, instruments or connected equipment as well as to software vendors. The practical difficulty is rarely the report itself; it is that a 24-hour clock requires a detection and decision path that most engineering organisations have never had to build.
